title: South Korean AI Tool Reads a Single ECG to Flag Post-Surgery Death Risk, Study Finds
excerpt: Researchers at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital analyzed over 41,000 patients and found that an AI-enhanced electrocardiogram could classify 92 percent of surgical candidates as low-risk, potentially eliminating unnecessary cardiac testing.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • AI tool classifies 92.3% of surgical candidates as low-risk for complications post-surgery.
  • Low-risk patients had a mere 0.2% adverse event rate compared to 2.9% for high-risk patients.
  • Only 16.3% of preoperative cardiovascular tests showed positive results, indicating overuse of testing.
  • The AI tool, 'ECG Buddy,' is now integrated into clinical workflows at the hospital.
  • The study suggests potential cost savings and efficiency in surgical patient management.

Study from Seoul National University Bundang Hospital
  • A study of 41,218 patients at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital found that an AI-powered ECG tool could classify 92.3 percent of noncardiac surgery candidates as low-risk for postoperative complications.
  • Low-risk patients identified by the AI had a composite adverse event rate of just 0.2 percent, compared to 2.9 percent for high-risk patients.
  • Only 16.3 percent of preoperative cardiovascular tests yielded positive findings, suggesting widespread overuse of conventional cardiac testing before surgery.
  • The tool, called "ECG Buddy," has been approved by South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety and is now integrated into the hospital's clinical workflow.

A deep-learning algorithm that analyzes a single standard electrocardiogram can accurately predict which patients face elevated mortality risk after noncardiac surgery, according to a study published in the Journal of Medical Internet Research by researchers at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital.

The retrospective cohort study, which analyzed 41,218 patients across 46,135 ECG-surgery pairs between 2020 and 2021, found that the AI tool classified 92.3 percent of surgical cases as low-risk. Those patients had a composite adverse event rate — covering 30-day all-cause mortality and unplanned percutaneous coronary intervention — of just 0.2 percent. High-risk patients, by contrast, had a rate of 2.9 percent.

Eliminating Unnecessary Tests

The study's most significant finding concerns the potential for reducing preoperative cardiac testing. Of the 5,458 cases that underwent advanced cardiovascular imaging before surgery — including echocardiography, coronary CT angiography, SPECT scans, and coronary angiography — only 16.3 percent yielded clinically positive results.

Among patients classified as low-risk by the AI, event rates remained uniformly low regardless of whether additional cardiac testing was performed, suggesting that much of the current preoperative testing regimen may be clinically unnecessary for the majority of patients.

The research team, led by Professor Cho Young-jin of the Department of Cardiology and Professor Kim Joong-hee of the Department of Emergency Medicine, developed the underlying AI system — a deep-learning platform called Quantitative ECG, or QCG — that uses standard 12-lead ECG images as input.

How the Technology Works

The QCG system employs a modified convolutional neural network with residual connections, squeeze excitation modules, and a nonlocal block. It was pretrained using self-supervised learning on 47,194 annotated ECG images recorded at SNUBH between 2017 and 2019, and fine-tuned through multitask learning to generate 10 digital biomarkers.

Among these, the QCG-Critical score — originally developed to identify patients at risk of shock, respiratory failure, or cardiac arrest — proved most predictive of postoperative outcomes. The tool has been commercialized as "ECG Buddy," an application that received Class 2 medical device certification from South Korea's Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.

Outperforming Conventional Risk Scores

Earlier validation studies showed the AI algorithm achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.83 for predicting post-procedural mortality — substantially outperforming the widely used Revised Cardiac Risk Index, which scored 0.67. The AI also maintained strong discrimination across different procedure types, including cardiac surgery, noncardiac surgery, and catheterization procedures.

Patients identified as high-risk by the model had an unadjusted odds ratio for postoperative mortality of 8.83, compared to 2.08 for patients with elevated conventional risk scores.

Implications for Global Healthcare

The study's conclusions carry particular weight for healthcare systems grappling with rising surgical volumes and constrained resources. Preoperative cardiac testing adds cost, delays surgery, and rarely changes clinical management for low-risk patients. An AI tool that can triage patients using a routine, inexpensive test completed in under a minute could meaningfully reduce healthcare spending.

For India's hospital networks, where surgical volumes are growing rapidly and preoperative cardiac testing is common, the SNUBH model offers a potential template. Indian health technology companies are increasingly developing their own AI-ECG platforms, and the South Korean research provides validation data that could accelerate adoption.

The researchers acknowledged the study's retrospective design as a limitation and called for prospective clinical trials to confirm the economic and clinical benefits before widespread adoption.
